extracted.intended_audience: general readers and prospective Stack Exchange community members (site proposers, moderators, active users)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures, thresholds, and expectations for proposing, launching, moderating, and operating sites in the Stack Exchange network (Area 51 process, beta/graduation criteria, moderator elections, bounties, reputation, licensing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area 51 Definition requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A public proposal must be drafted and posted so that any member of the community can discuss the proposal and vote on it. The proposal must address these four key issues: the topic of the site; the targeted audience; forty exemplary questions, upvoted at least 10 times from the community; 60 followers from the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows a collaborative proposal to emerge over time; exemplary questions should be high-quality and receive community upvotes to demonstrate interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area 51 Commitment requirements (participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, 200 users interested in the new site are asked to formally commit and support the site by actively participating and contributing to it by asking or answering 10 questions during the six months of the public beta. Second, 100 users interested in the new site that have committed with over 200 reputation on another site on the network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commitments are intended to ensure an initial active user base who will ask/answer during beta; committed users should be prepared to contribute the specified number of posts during the beta period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area 51 Commitment score threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: A commitment score of 500 is required for progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives the precise scoring components (see Commitment score formula entry) used to compute whether a proposal reaches the required commitment score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment scoring formula (PrelimScore & UserScore)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula quantifies each committers' effective contribution to the commitment score, weighting reputation and recency (DAYS) to compute site-wide commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beta phases and minimum durations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the concept receives 100% commitment (reaches the requirements listed above), the site enters the private beta phase. Private Beta must remain for at least 35 days. Public Beta: The site is open to the public for a long period; it must remain for at least 180 days (or 6 months) of public beta, and 215 total days of beta (31 weeks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-step beta (private then public) is intended to let committed members test and grow the community before full launch; minimum durations are enforced to allow critical-mass signals to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: If the site has at least 1000 open questions, and 70% of questions or more have at least 1 upvoted answer, it is granted a 'graduation' and fully launched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These quantitative thresholds (open question count and percent of questions with an upvoted answer) are used as signals of sustained activity and answer quality before granting full site status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderator nomination eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To become a moderator, users have to participate in an election. Users must first nominate themselves and have at least 300 reputation (3,000 on Stack Overflow and 1,000 on Math Stack Exchange), while also being in good standing, such as not having been suspended during the past year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nominating users must introduce themselves, explain why they would be a good moderator, and answer community-written questions; nominations can be withdrawn at any time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderator election process and advancement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: After nominations, users vote on the candidates in a primary, where the vote tally is made public. The top 10 nominees advance to the election stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public primary narrows the slate; transparency of tallies is part of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election voting eligibility and counting method
rubrics_metrics.description: In the election stage any user with at least 150 reputation is allowed to vote. A ranked-choice voting system is used where users can rank all the candidates if they wish. Votes are tallied using the Meek STV method (single transferable vote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meek STV allows fractional parts of a vote to be counted; the system supports ranked-choice preferences and proportional selection of moderators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderator responsibilities and behavioral expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderators are responsible for managing the site, such as by following up on flagged posts, locking and protecting posts, suspending users, and deleting the worst posts (including misinformation). According to the Stack Exchange philosophy, they should be minimally involved in the site. They are also expected to lead by example, as well as to show respect to other users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderators act as exception-handlers and community leaders; 'minimal involvement' emphasizes community self-moderation with moderators stepping in primarily for exceptional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounty rules and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties can be applied on questions 48 hours after being asked, lasting for 7 days plus a grace period of 24 hours. The minimum bounty is set at 50 reputation, except if the user has already answered the question or has offered a previous bounty on the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bounties are a mechanism to donate reputation to attract attention or better answers; timing and minimum amounts are fixed by these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounty non-cancellation and non-refund rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties cannot be cancelled, and reputation cannot be refunded from a bounty, even if the question did not receive an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once offered, the reputation cost is final—this encourages careful use of bounties and prevents strategic rescinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation system and privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Users can vote on both answers and questions, and through this process users earn reputation points. Users receive privileges by collecting reputation points, ranging from the ability to vote and comment on questions and answers to the ability to moderate many aspects of the site. Badges are awarded for asking and answering, participating in meta, and for moderating the site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation and badges form the primary gamified mechanisms enabling community self-moderation and gradual unlocking of privileges; the system is compared to Digg in its early release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content licensing of user contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: User contributions since May 2, 2018 are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0). Older content, contributed while the site used CC BY-SA 3.0 or 2.5, remains licensed under the license in force at the time it was contributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing changes and relicensing have been a source of community concern and discussion; the page notes user puzzlement and debate around the 2019 change to reference CC BY-SA 4.0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site-topic selection (critical mass) via Area 51 voting/algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Users vote on new site topics in a staging area called Area 51, where algorithms determine which suggested site topics have critical mass and should be created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community voting plus algorithmic thresholds together decide whether a proposal has sufficient interest ('critical mass') to proceed through the site-creation pipeline.
